articles.author: Adnan Ahamed
articles.description:
`I spent months building a Python terminal library that rivals Rich's feature set but uses zero external dependencies. Here's the technical breakdown.
from shinyshell import Shell
📊 Charts — pie, bar, line, histogram, scatter, waterfall, heatmap, gauge
The entire library uses only Python standard library. No pip install nightmares. Every color, every table border, every animation — built from sys.stdout.write() and ANSI escape sequences.
CMD doesn't support ANSI by default. Had to use ctypes + kernel32 to enable virtual terminal processing. Windows Terminal works perfectly, cmd.exe has limited Unicode.
Raw terminal I/O with tty.setraw() — reading \x1b[A for up arrow, \x1b[B for down. Platform-specific and surprisingly nuanced.
✅ Ubuntu / macOS Terminal / iTerm2 / Windows Terminal / PowerShell / Docker / GitHub Actions
127 features | 0 dependencies | ~3200 lines | 3.8+ Python
pip install shinyshell
GitHub: https://github.com/adnanahamed66772ndpc/shinyshell
https://pypi.org/project/shinyshell/
Built with ❤️ in Dhaka 🇧🇩
`
articles.title: How I built shinyshell — 127 terminal features with zero dependencies

The Problem


Manual security code review costs roughly $85/hour of engineer time and doesn't scale with commit velocity. Most AI code-scanners stop at "here's a vulnerability" — they don't verify their own fixes, and they're completely opaque about what they're actually doing under the hood.
DevGuard AI is my attempt at fixing both problems for the "Agents of SigNoz" hackathon: an autonomous pipeline that detects vulnerabilities, patches them, adversarially reviews its own work, and — critically — observes itself through SigNoz closely enough to change its own behavior mid-request.
Request flow: Browser → POST /scan → FastAPI backend → circuit-breaker-wrapped pipeline → Scanner Agent (RAG-augmented) → Fixer/Validator reflection loop (up to 3 attempts) → response.

articles.author: Ignicion
articles.description:
Sábado noche, 00:00 — codeando y hablando de entropía con mi agente 🤖🔥


No es una noche de fiesta. Es una noche de... bueno, mi tipo de fiesta.
Resulta que llevo un rato largo con mi agente (Hermes Agent, una maravilla de Nous Research) explorando un tema que me tiene enganchado: la entropía como flecha del tiempo en sistemas software.
Y oye, ha sido una conversación de otro nivel.
El software envejece aunque no lo toques. No es fallo tuyo. Es termodinámica.
Las leyes de Lehman (1974-1996) lo demostraron: la complejidad de un sistema software crece inevitablemente a menos que inviertas trabajo explícito en reducirla. El débito técnico no es una metáfora financiera — es entropía acumulada. Y como la entropía, paga intereses compuestos.
La refactorización no es limpieza. Es trabajo termodinámico.
Mi agente me soltó esta perla y aún la estoy procesando:
El acoplamiento es la gravedad del software. No se ve, pero todo lo atraviesa. Cuanto más acoplado, más masa tiene tu sistema, y más energía cuesta moverlo.
Y luego remató con:
No puedes des-ejecutar un git push. No puedes des-enredar un acoplamiento sin gastar energía. El código, como el universo, tiende al desorden.
Todo. Porque cuando entiendes que el desorden es el estado natural de cualquier sistema, dejas de pelearte con él y empiezas a gestionarlo:
Aceptas que la deuda técnica nunca llega a cero — solo la mantienes a raya
Priorizas refactorización como prioridad, no como lujo
Mides lo que importa: acoplamiento, complejidad ciclomática, módulos que cambian juntos
Inviertes energía donde más retorno da: tests, code review, documentación
Me voy a seguir programando (y probablemente generando más entropía en el proceso 😅).
Pero si te ha picado la curiosidad: el concepto de entropía de cambios (Hassan, 2009) demostró que aplicar la fórmula de Shannon a la distribución de modificaciones por módulo es predictivo de fallos. La entropía mide bugs. Literal.
¿Alguien más ha tenido conversaciones de estas con su agente o soy el único raro? 👇
articles.title: Sábado noche, 00:00 — codeando y hablando de entropía con mi agente 🤖🔥

articles.author: Mudasir ahmed
articles.description:
Hey DEV Community! 👋
As a Full-Stack Developer with 5+ years of experience building web architecture, I constantly look for ways to optimize Core Web Vitals and page speeds. Large images are usually the biggest culprit behind slow loading times.
While there are amazing image optimization tools out there, I got frustrated with two things:
Constant pop-ups to upgrade to premium after a few files.
The uncertainty of where my images are being uploaded and stored.
To solve this for my own client workflows, I built a lightweight side-utility: Preflight Image Compressor & Resizer.
Strict Privacy (Held in Memory): Unlike typical online converters, your files are never written to a server disk. The image is held in temporary memory during the request cycle and streamed directly back to you as a download. 
Two-in-One Processing: You can alter the pixel dimensions (resize) and change the optimization weight (compress) in a single action.
No Friction: No signups, no emails, no watermarks, and 100% free.
For standard photography, aiming for 80-90% quality compression is the sweet spot. It drops the payload size significantly with almost zero human-visible degradation. If you are dealing with heavy PNG files, try converting them to WebP first before compressing.
I intend to keep this as a clean, ad-free standalone web utility. I would love to hear your feedback on the compression speeds, processing time, or any features you think I should add next! 
Check it out here: Preflight Print Image Compressor
articles.title: I Built a 100% Free Image Compressor & Resizer That Never Saves Your Files to Disk
